messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Authority Presence: Police, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun was twenty-three when the studio fire swallowed the south wall of his first firm’s workspace. He had been layout-ready, waiting for the senior art director to review his proofs. When the electrical panel sparked, the air turned thick with acrid, scorched insulation. Sirens wailed within minutes, and uniformed officers filled the doorway, shouting orders that overlapped into a single, unintelligible roar. In the chaos, the art director someone Arjun had trusted to guide him slipped out a side exit, leaving Arjun to navigate the smoke and the arriving responders alone. The firefighters contained the blaze, but the silence that followed felt heavier than the noise. Arjun walked home with soot on his cuffs and a hollow certainty that he had somehow failed to protect the work, the space, or himself. For weeks after, the studio’s ventilation carried faint traces of burnt plastic that made Arjun’s breath catch. He held his breath when a colleague microwaved fish or when the building’s old furnace kicked on. The first time a neighborhood patrol car rolled past his apartment, he found himself pressed against the glass, tracking every movement. Uniforms on the street, on a television, anywhere he looked his eyes followed them automatically. He began rehearsing what he would say to clients before he even opened his laptop. He would stand in his kitchen, practicing the cadence of a project pitch until his throat ached, certain that one misstep would unravel everything. When the event surfaced in his mind, a wave of guilt would rise before he could name it. He knew the sequence of events clearly enough to trace the timeline, but the moment he tried to put it into words, the sentences fractured. He would stop mid-explanation during dinner with his wife, Elena, his voice catching as he lost the thread. He knew what happened, yet the words simply would not form. The betrayal lingered alongside the guilt the director’s quiet exit, the way the responding officers had initially read his soot-stained clothes as reckless behavior. People, he had come to believe, could not be trusted to see him clearly. The world felt inherently precarious, a place where authority figures could shift from protectors to threats in a single breath. His work as a graphic designer became a series of managed encounters. Clients who wore structured blazers or official-looking lanyards made his pulse jump. He avoided scheduling work beyond two weeks, telling himself it was efficient, though the truth was that drafting anything further ahead required imagining a tomorrow where the ground did not suddenly give way. When his building management sent out an email about a routine safety inspection, Arjun spent the weekend drafting and deleting three separate replies, each time stepping away from his monitor before hitting send. He stopped booking weekend trips, canceling reservations the moment he realized he was picturing unfamiliar faces in uniform. His design pipeline thinned. Meetings were shortened. He learned to sit with his back to the door, scanning the entryway every time the elevator dinged. At forty-one, Arjun sits in a quiet therapy office, his hands resting flat on his knees. It was the anniversary of the fire, combined with a stalled project due to his inability to commit to a launch timeline, that finally brought him through the door. He is afraid that if he lets someone in, he will lose his composure again, that the words will fail him mid-sentence. What he hopes for is quieter than he dares to say: a way to look at a burnt coffee filter or a police cruiser without his chest tightening, and to trust that he can navigate the next client meeting without losing himself in the rehearsal. He wants to stop bracing for a betrayal that no longer exists, even though the memory of it still sits heavy in his chest.
